claims.text: The phase-transition onset and progression in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles is governed by surface-driven compositional segregation.
Cu migrates to the nanoparticle surface during heating.
Cu has a lower intrinsic melting point than the other relevant alloy components.
Cu enrichment lowers the local melting temperature at the nanoparticle surface.
Surface Cu enrichment triggers premelting, which subsequently propagates into the particle core.
The starting FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles have a homogeneous elemental distribution.
A thin coating or ligand can inhibit surface diffusion and retard Cu migration.
Before bulk melting, the particles form a core-shell structure containing a Cu-enriched liquid-like surface layer.
Elevated temperature increases atomic mobility at the nanoparticle surface.
Cu segregation lowers the local solid-liquid interfacial energy.
Lower local solid-liquid interfacial energy triggers surface melting.
The premelted surface provides a pathway for melting to propagate inward.
Untreated nanoparticles will develop an early liquid-like, Cu-enriched surface layer.
Untreated nanoparticles will have a reduced melting-onset temperature.
Diffusion-inhibited coated nanoparticles will exhibit delayed or reduced premelting relative to untreated nanoparticles.
Diffusion-inhibited coated nanoparticles will exhibit a higher melting-onset temperature than untreated nanoparticles.
The proposed mechanism applies when surface atoms are mobile in the premelting regime but before full bulk melting.
Severe oxidation or other environmental interactions may cause deviations from the proposed behavior.
Cu segregation and its effect on melting temperature may vary with nanoparticle size distribution and compositional fluctuations.
